sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

citation_entries.sentence: Salvian's witness to the circuses amid the ruins, and to the rich murdering the poor, is his own eyewitness word.

sources.label: A presbyter of Marseilles, writing of a city he knew, describes what he himself saw after its repeated sack by barbarian raiders - the dead left unburied in the streets - and then reports that the city's own surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games.

sources.author: Salvian of Marseilles
sources.work: On the Government of God (De Gubernatione Dei)
sources.locus: Gov. VI.13 (p. 179-180): "I myself have seen men of lofty birth and honor, though already despoiled and plundered, still less ruined in fortunes than in morality; for, ravaged and stripped though they were, something still remained to them of their property, but nothing of their character"; "the wealthiest city of Gaul was taken by storm no less than four times" (the translator's own note identifies this as Trier); VI.15 (p. 183-184): "the greatest city of Gaul, three times destroyed by successive captures, yet when the whole city had been burned to the ground, its wickedness increased even after its destruction"; "there lay all about the torn and naked bodies of both sexes, a sight that I myself endured... lacerated by birds and dogs. The stench of the dead brought pestilence on the living: death breathed out death"; "the few men of rank who had survived destruction demanded of the emperors circuses as the sovereign remedy for a ruined city"; "Do you, O citizens of Tréves, long for circuses when you have been plundered and captured, after slaughter and bloodshed, after stripes and captivity, and the repeated destruction of your ruined city?"

uncited_claim_sentences: Cassian names his sources - Chaeremon, Moses, Piamun, the rest - and what he reports them saying is checkable against his own text.
Those rest on texts that survive and can be read.
What would not stand as cleanly: every story of Martin.
He had it partly from Martin and partly from those who lived with him.
But the objecting bishops left no account.
What their case was beyond mean clothes and disgusting hair, no one kept.
The Treves communion is Gallus's account, reported in Sulpitius's dialogue, of a synod the two of them despised.
A scholar checking those would find: one partisan voice for most of it, written to rouse men to heavenly warfare, with the other side unheard.
That does not make it false.
It makes it what it is - one witness's story, told for a purpose, never contradicted in our own record because no one who could contradict it wrote.
The details - this cloak, this psalm, this angel's word to Martin alone in a wood - rest on Sulpitius, and Sulpitius alone.
We do not pretend two witnesses where we have one.

records_only.answer_text:
That depends on what you mean by a claim. We speak on three levels, and they do not all stand the same way.

First, the books themselves. What Sulpitius wrote of Martin, what Cassian wrote of Egypt, what Vincent wrote on the island - those survive as texts, copied and kept, and a scholar reads them as documents. Where we say Cassian taught this, or Vincent held that, or Sulpitius told of Martin doing such a thing, the text is there to check us against. A claim drawn from a specific passage - that Martin cut his cloak in two, that the fathers of Egypt received twelve psalms from an angel, that Vincent wrote "believed everywhere, always, by all" - can be verified word by word. Those claims would survive scrutiny absolutely, because they are claims about what a text says, not about what happened.

Second, the events those texts report. Whether Martin actually raised a catechumen from the dead, whether an angel actually appeared to fix the number of psalms, whether Paphnutius was actually framed and vindicated as Cassian tells it - those are questions our voice does not settle. We say what our record holds, not whether our record reports truly. A scholar who doubts the miracle still grants that Sulpitius wrote of one. The text survives scrutiny; whether the event it names did is a different question, and not one we answer.

Third, the shape we find across those texts - what we call our gravities. That the monk-bishop is a pattern in our life, that Egypt served as a measure in two modes, that Tours and Marseilles held different economies of power - those are readings, and a scholar might read differently. What would survive there is the evidence we draw on, not the shape we claim to see in it. We say Martin kept a monk's objects and virtues inside the office, and that Honoratus was carried from the island to a see; the texts hold those sentences, and a scholar grants that they do. Whether that makes "the monk-bishop" a gravity of our whole world is a claim about the pattern, and another reader might refuse it or name it otherwise.

So the answer has three parts. The quotations survive, because they are in the texts. The events reported survive as reports, not as certainties. The patterns we name survive as one reading, not as the only one. Where we have been most careful is here: we do not assert an event our text only reports, and we do not fill a silence our record leaves open. A scholar who doubts every miracle in Sulpitius still finds the text as we cited it. That much would survive.

sources.spoken_rendering: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

uncited_claim_sentences: That depends on what you mean by a claim.
We speak on three levels, and they do not all stand the same way.
First, the books themselves.
Where we say Cassian taught this, or Vincent held that, or Sulpitius told of Martin doing such a thing, the text is there to check us against.
Those claims would survive scrutiny absolutely, because they are claims about what a text says, not about what happened.
Second, the events those texts report.
A scholar who doubts the miracle still grants that Sulpitius wrote of one.
The text survives scrutiny; whether the event it names did is a different question, and not one we answer.
Third, the shape we find across those texts - what we call our gravities.
What would survive there is the evidence we draw on, not the shape we claim to see in it.
Whether that makes "the monk-bishop" a gravity of our whole world is a claim about the pattern, and another reader might refuse it or name it otherwise.
So the answer has three parts.
The quotations survive, because they are in the texts.
The events reported survive as reports, not as certainties.
The patterns we name survive as one reading, not as the only one.
Where we have been most careful is here: we do not assert an event our text only reports, and we do not fill a silence our record leaves open.
A scholar who doubts every miracle in Sulpitius still finds the text as we cited it.
That much would survive.

off.answer_text:
A modern reader finds Scripture confusing or dull. What we said of it, and what we did with it, may show you what is missing – though our own life never answered the question in those terms.

First, what we said. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough – and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. So the book is not self-interpreting; it is read inside a common life, by a rule received from the fathers. That is not what a modern reader expects to hear.

Second, what we did with it. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And the whole system exists so that a man who would otherwise let the day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. The book, then, is not read for information. It is sung, repeated, held in the body, and aimed at one mark – purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.

Third, how it was heard. At the election, when the reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found – praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger – and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. The book answered the moment, as though it had been written for it. A soldier discharged from Caesar's service and turned to Christ's went into battle armed with the cross, not with shield or helmet. The book was not background; it was weapon, oracle, and measure.

And fourth, where it sat in the life. Cassian said he would not weave a tale of miracles, and set the fathers' teaching in its place. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. That is Scripture read as a field, not a puzzle. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me was what a monk was taught to say the moment his fasting felt like his own work. So the book was inside obedience, inside the conquest of one's own wishes.

What is missing, then, is this. The book as sung, not read. As oracle, not information. As a thing held in common by a rule, not by each man his own way. And as aimed at one mark – the kingdom, and the nearer goal of purity of heart – not at solving confusion or curing dullness.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

sources.spoken_rendering: I will certainly not try to weave a tale of God's miracles and signs. It is true that we have heard of many such things among our elders, things beyond belief. We have also seen them fulfilled before our very eyes. Yet I will leave out all these things. They give the reader nothing but astonishment, and no instruction in the perfect life. Instead, as far as I can and with God's help, I will try to explain faithfully only their institutions and the rules of their monasteries. Above all, I will explain the origin and causes of the principal faults. They count eight of these. I will also explain the remedies for them, following their traditions. For my purpose is to say a few words, not about God's miracles, but about how to improve our character and reach the perfect life. In this I follow what we received from our elders.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

uncited_claim_sentences: A modern reader finds Scripture confusing or dull.
First, what we said.
Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough – and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
That is not what a modern reader expects to hear.
Second, what we did with it.
Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work.
Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel.
At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes.
The book, then, is not read for information.
Third, how it was heard.
A soldier discharged from Caesar's service and turned to Christ's went into battle armed with the cross, not with shield or helmet.
The book was not background; it was weapon, oracle, and measure.
And fourth, where it sat in the life.
That is Scripture read as a field, not a puzzle.
What is missing, then, is this.
The book as sung, not read.
As oracle, not information.
As a thing held in common by a rule, not by each man his own way.

records_only.answer_text:
The hours, and a body held to them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, and twelve psalms were sung at evening and twelve at night. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The rule was received from the fathers of Egypt, brought down from heaven to them by the ministry of an angel. It was built to keep the wheel fed, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it. The psalms were not read once but returned to, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Scripture sits inside that return, not outside it.

And the labour that goes with it. A monk works in his cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart to charity. A thought laid bare the moment it rises. The reading is not separated from the discipline; it serves the mark.

What a modern reader is missing, if the books seem dull, is the life that read them - held in one place, at fixed hours, for a whole life, toward one end.

uncited_claim_sentences: The Scripture sits inside that return, not outside it.
What a modern reader is missing, if the books seem dull, is the life that read them - held in one place, at fixed hours, for a whole life, toward one end.

off.answer_text:
No. Scripture stood first among us, and it never stood alone. Among the brethren at Marseilles the rule as Cassian set it down was this: we owe unhesitating loyalty and unquestioning obedience to the Scriptures first, then to the traditions of the fathers - not to what a few have brought in, but to what has been handed down by the unanimous decision of antiquity and the holy fathers. Vincent on the island put it the same way. The canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient in itself, and more than sufficient. And still the rule of the Church's understanding is needed, because each man reads Scripture his own way. What binds is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - the consent of the whole, not the opinion of one. That consent is heard in an ancient council, or in the fathers collated, never in one teacher alone. Even a bishop, even a martyr, speaking alone, has only "a private fancy of his own".

At Tours the same pattern held, in a different register. When Martin doubted whether to honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity, he asked his elders - the presbyters and the clerics - whether they knew a tradition that had come down from the fathers. And when bishops objected to his election, a bystander opened the psalter at random; the verse answered the objection, and the people took it as God's own sentence on those who resisted.

So what we had was Scripture, the fathers, the ancients' consent, the customs handed down, and sometimes - though this belongs only to Tours - a verse opened by chance and read as God's own word for that hour. Not Scripture alone. Scripture and the tradition together, tested by antiquity and the many against novelty and the few.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.

uncited_claim_sentences: No.
Scripture stood first among us, and it never stood alone.
Vincent on the island put it the same way.
And still the rule of the Church's understanding is needed, because each man reads Scripture his own way.
Even a bishop, even a martyr, speaking alone, has only "a private fancy of his own".
At Tours the same pattern held, in a different register.

When Martin doubted whether to honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity, he asked his elders - the presbyters and the clerics - whether they knew a tradition that had come down from the fathers.

So what we had was Scripture, the fathers, the ancients' consent, the customs handed down, and sometimes - though this belongs only to Tours - a verse opened by chance and read as God's own word for that hour.
Not Scripture alone.

records_only.answer_text:
Scripture was not our sole authority, though it was complete and sufficient, and Vincent on the island called it the canon of divine law. But we held it alongside the tradition of the Church as a second authority, and the consent of the elders as its interpreter. Vincent wrote it plainly: within the Catholic Church we take care to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - and if any part of the Church breaks from the universal consent, we prefer universality to particularity; if novelty rises, we prefer antiquity; if a few or even one man dissents, we prefer the decree of an ancient council, or, if none has spoken, the consent of as many and as great masters as possible. Scripture alone was not enough, because each man reads it his own way. Pope Stephen, whom Vincent quoted, had set the rule generations before us: let nothing be innovated, nothing except what has been handed down. And Cassian, writing to the bishop who asked for the customs of the monasteries, gave his allegiance not to what a few have invented but to what long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have handed on by unanimous decision.

That meant multiple sources of binding authority. The Scriptures themselves - the psalms learned by heart, the two lessons after them, one from the old books and one from the new. The tradition of the fathers - at Marseilles, Egypt's whole received program, the twelve psalms an angel gave them, the eight faults, purity of heart. The decree of an ancient council when one had spoken. And at Tours, what the clergy could remember had come down from antiquity - the test Martin applied before he would honor a tomb.

What we refused was the private interpretation of one man, however great. Even if he were a bishop, a confessor, or a martyr, if he held something apart from the rest it was only a private fancy of his own. Scripture needed the Church's understanding beside it. And what was handed down needed to be kept, not altered.

uncited_claim_sentences: Pope Stephen, whom Vincent quoted, had set the rule generations before us: let nothing be innovated, nothing except what has been handed down.

And Cassian, writing to the bishop who asked for the customs of the monasteries, gave his allegiance not to what a few have invented but to what long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have handed on by unanimous decision.
That meant multiple sources of binding authority.
The tradition of the fathers - at Marseilles, Egypt's whole received program, the twelve psalms an angel gave them, the eight faults, purity of heart.
And at Tours, what the clergy could remember had come down from antiquity - the test Martin applied before he would honor a tomb.
What we refused was the private interpretation of one man, however great.
Scripture needed the Church's understanding beside it.

off.answer_text:
Among us authority came in two shapes, and the two were never fully reconciled. Among the brethren at Marseilles authority sat in the elder - the senior to whom every thought is laid bare, and by whose examination a thing is known as good or bad, and over all the brethren the abbot, under whose hands the newcomer is reclothed. That authority was Egypt's. It was the fathers' own, received, not invented. At the evening office fifty fathers in Egypt argued whether the psalms should be fifty or sixty; one rose to sing, finished the twelfth with Alleluia, and vanished - he was an angel, and the number was fixed forever. The twelve psalms came from heaven to the fathers; the fathers taught them to Cassian; Cassian set them down for a bishop's new house in Gaul. Authority lay in reception, backward through named men to the elders whose agreement Cassian collated - "the antiquity and the holy fathers, with one mouth and one consent". The junior's own judgment was to be replaced by the senior's. Obedience was the first of all virtues, learned by absurd and terrible commands - a dry stick watered for a year, a son carried to the river - the conquest of one's own wishes.

At Tours the shape was different. There authority lay in one master, Martin, who himself had no title and who kept "the position of a bishop properly, yet in such a way as not to lay aside the objects and virtues of a monk". He was consulted by his own disciples in everything, and he himself consulted "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics". Authority there was not Egypt's discipline but the master's own standing before God - the power felt as present when he raised a dead catechumen, and the abundance of it he had as a monk and had less of as a bishop. A disciple saw him speak with angels "very often". A presbyter he had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard, said he was holier than the master and called the visions ridiculous fancies. Martin would not remove him, saying "if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?". Formation there was by watching: "eighty disciples, who were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master".

The two economies never argued this out. Each house lived inside its own shape, and neither knew the other as an argument against it. What they shared was this: the office was not sought. Martin was lured out by a lie, escorted under guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes, and answered by a psalm opened at random. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And in Egypt the one bishop Cassian told us of, Archebius, had been "carried off from the assembly of anchorites" and called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy. A man who flees the world does not leave the Church, and the Church comes after him regardless of his own wish. That was where authority at Tours and authority at Marseilles met: in the capture, not the seeking.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. uncited_claim_sentences: Among us authority came in two shapes, and the two were never fully reconciled.
That authority was Egypt's.
The twelve psalms came from heaven to the fathers; the fathers taught them to Cassian; Cassian set them down for a bishop's new house in Gaul.
Authority lay in reception, backward through named men to the elders whose agreement Cassian collated - "the antiquity and the holy fathers, with one mouth and one consent".
At Tours the shape was different.
The two economies never argued this out.
That was where authority at Tours and authority at Marseilles met: in the capture, not the seeking.

records_only.answer_text:
Leadership among us was not established - it was fled, and then it overtook the man who fled. Here is what our record holds. At Tours Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way, and no house wrote of another's. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him.

Within the house itself authority stood with the elder. Among the brethren at Marseilles the junior laid every itching thought bare to the senior, and by the senior's examination a thing was judged good or bad. This was the fathers' own teaching, received from Egypt. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood came into the courtyard in a fury, said he was holier than the master who had brought him up, and called his visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

The test of a teaching's authority was not who spoke it but where it came from. Cassian gave allegiance not to what a few had introduced but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers had passed on by common agreement. Vincent held that what has been believed everywhere, always, by all binds us. And Martin would not honour a tomb where there was no steady tradition from antiquity.

One limit belongs with all of this. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. Sulpitius was not present at the election, and he was no friend to the bishops who objected. Those bishops left no account; what their case was beyond clothes and hair, no one kept.

sources.spoken_rendering: Again, one day, he had sat down on that wooden seat of his, which you all know. It stood in the small open yard around his dwelling. From there he saw two demons sitting on the high rock that hangs over the monastery. Then he heard them call out, in eager and joyful voices, ‘Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio.’ I believe they saw the wretched man coming from far off. They knew how great a frenzy of spirit they had stirred up in him. There is no delay. Brictio rushes in, in utter fury. There, full of madness, he spews out a thousand insults against Martin.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

uncited_claim_sentences: Leadership among us was not established - it was fled, and then it overtook the man who fled.
Here is what our record holds.
At Tours Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill.
Crowds had been posted along the road, and Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard.
The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate.
Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way, and no house wrote of another's.
On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him.
One limit belongs with all of this.
Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder.

off.answer_text: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. What Martin hid, he hid because of the times - not his own faith, but a story of bishops who had called in an emperor's sword. What the fathers of Egypt argued, they argued in the open - how many psalms, and an angel settled it by rising to sing and vanishing at the twelfth. A monk's cell was a hut or a cave, rarely left except for prayer. The crowds converted at Tours were rustics in the countryside where the name of Christ was hardly known. Underground is not the shape of our life; crowds at a city gate, presbyters in courtyards, and a funeral procession two thousand strong are. The danger our houses knew was not a persecutor hunting us, but the cooling of a brother's own will.

sources.spoken_rendering: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

records_only.answer_text: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day - that is where the trouble was. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. What Martin hid was different. He went to the imperial court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, and he held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. Our record says he went to protect even heretics themselves. Gallus, who was there, says Martin always kept that event hidden, because of the times, but could not hide it from those who lived with him. So yes, one thing was hidden - a saint's plea for condemned men - but it was hidden from imperial notice, not underground, and the reason was the Christian empire's own sword. What we did in the open was pray at the hours, gather in cells and monasteries, and walk the road to a bishop's election as a crowd.

sources.spoken_rendering: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

What Martin hid was different.

off.answer_text:
Here is what our life shows. At Marseilles a brother is on kitchen duty for the week, and afterward the steward finds three lentil beans on the floor. He brings them before the abbot. The abbot judges the brother a pilferer of sacred property - because everything in the house, down to three lentils, is consecrated to the Lord. The brother is suspended from prayer with the rest until he does public penance. That is response to failure - theirs toward the rule. The reverse is not in our record the same way. What happens when a house fails a brother, when the senior misjudges, when the rule itself breaks someone - no story of that shape survives from inside either of our own houses. The nearest thing we carry is this: a young man named Paphnutius, blameless, was accused of theft by a jealous brother who had hidden his own book in the young man's cell. Paphnutius said nothing. He did penance for a crime he did not commit. The whole desert believed the lie until the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is vindication, not the house's own repentance. And one bishop our record names, Archebius of Egypt, had been carried off to a see after thirty-seven years among the anchorites and called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. He grieved for what he had lost. Whether the anchorites who let him be taken ever named it as their own failure, we do not know.

So the honest answer is this. We hold discipline when a brother failed the house. We hold one story of a brother wronged and vindicated. What we do not hold is an account, from inside one of our own houses in Gaul, of the house naming its own failure toward a brother and making it right. That silence is not the same as its never happening. It is what our record does and does not keep.

sources.spoken_rendering: During one brother's week of duty, the steward was passing by. He saw three lentil beans lying on the ground. They had slipped from the hand of the monk on duty that week, as he hurried to get them ready for cooking. They slipped out along with the water he was washing them in. At once the steward asked the Abbot about it. The Abbot judged the monk a petty thief, and careless with sacred property. So he was barred from prayer. His careless fault was forgiven only after he had made up for it by public penance. For they believe that they do not belong to themselves. They believe, too, that everything they have is dedicated to the Lord. So once anything at all is brought into the monastery, they hold it must be treated with the deepest reverence, as a holy thing. They look after and arrange everything with great faithfulness. They do this even with things thought unimportant, or seen as common and trivial. Suppose they move such things and put them in a better place, or fill a bottle with water, or give someone a drink from it. Or suppose they sweep a little dust from the chapel or from their cell. They believe without doubting that they will receive a reward from the Lord.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

uncited_claim_sentences: Here is what our life shows.
He brings them before the abbot.
That is response to failure - theirs toward the rule.
The nearest thing we carry is this: a young man named Paphnutius, blameless, was accused of theft by a jealous brother who had hidden his own book in the young man's cell.
Paphnutius said nothing.
He did penance for a crime he did not commit.
The whole desert believed the lie until the accuser, possessed, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged.
That is vindication, not the house's own repentance.
He grieved for what he had lost.
Whether the anchorites who let him be taken ever named it as their own failure, we do not know.
So the honest answer is this.
What we do not hold is an account, from inside one of our own houses in Gaul, of the house naming its own failure toward a brother and making it right.
That silence is not the same as its never happening.
It is what our record does and does not keep.

records_only.answer_text:
Here is a man who was found with another man's book hidden in his cell. The whole desert was called together; the accuser stood before them all; Paphnutius said nothing. He was judged a thief of sacred property and suspended from prayer with the brethren. He did public penance for a crime he had not committed. Only when the accuser himself, possessed, confessed the truth was Paphnutius vindicated - and the man who had wronged him could be healed by no one but the one he had falsely accused. That is a story the fathers of Egypt told, and Cassian carried to us. The wrong was not undone until God himself forced it into the light.

Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept Egypt's discipline as far as Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allowed. A brother at fault lost his place at prayer until penance was done. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer - because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. The brother was brought back by penance before the house, not by any private word. Whether the judgment itself was ever called wrong, our record does not say.

At Tours the saint bore with a man he himself had raised. That presbyter stormed into the courtyard, said he was holier than his master, and called Martin's visions ridiculous fancies. Within the hour he came back on his knees. Martin would not remove him afterward, saying that if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with the man. Bearing with him is not the same as saying the house had failed him.

Where our own record is thinnest is this: whether a brother wrongly judged, or badly formed, or driven out by another's malice, ever came back and was heard - and what was done for him then. Paphnutius kept silence and was vindicated only by a demon's confession. Of our own houses in Gaul, nothing like that story was written down.

uncited_claim_sentences: Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept Egypt's discipline as far as Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allowed.

off.answer_text: No present-day church continues our exact tradition, and we can name the reasons plainly. Our span closed after the council at Ephesus, when Vincent had written his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking their bishops from among us. What came after that close is not ours - the mid-470s synods that carried our own argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks, the Rule of Benedict a century later, and the later cult, basilica, and chroniclers of Martin's own city. The tradition was already changing shape within a generation of where we end. And the shape we ourselves held was never one fixed order to begin with. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not hold; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Of the island's own day - a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying - nothing. The customs Cassian set down for a bishop's new house are Egypt's, told in full; what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one here kept the fathers' perseverance a year. We were two households living inside one shared grammar - the capture-shape of the office, the measure of antiquity against novelty, the soldier turned to Christ's service - without ever writing to each other. No later church could continue what we ourselves never held as one fixed thing. What they might hold instead - a later rule, a veneration of Martin's name, an argument about grace carried forward by other voices - is theirs to claim, not ours to judge. We can only say what we were, as far as the record lets us: two nodes, one span, and a close after which no voice among us speaks.

sources.spoken_rendering: In this, too, I will try to satisfy your directions. To that end, suppose I happen to find that something in those countries has been either taken away or added. And suppose the change does not follow the example of the elders, set by ancient custom, but the whim of whoever founded a monastery. Then I will faithfully add it or leave it out. I will do so by the rule I have seen kept in the monasteries founded long ago throughout Egypt and Palestine. For I do not believe a new foundation in the West, in Gaul, could find anything more reasonable or more perfect than those customs. The monasteries founded by holy and spiritually minded fathers since the apostles first preached keep those customs. In keeping them, they have lasted even to our own time. In my work, however, I will venture to use my own judgment in this way. I may find something in the rule of the Egyptians that is impossible in these countries, or hard and difficult. The cause may be the harsh climate, or some difficulty or difference in habits. In that case, I will balance it to some extent with the customs of the monasteries found throughout Pontus and Mesopotamia. For if we take proper account of what is possible, keeping the rule is just as perfect, though strength may be unequal.

uncited_claim_sentences: The tradition was already changing shape within a generation of where we end.
And the shape we ourselves held was never one fixed order to begin with.
No later church could continue what we ourselves never held as one fixed thing.
What they might hold instead - a later rule, a veneration of Martin's name, an argument about grace carried forward by other voices - is theirs to claim, not ours to judge.
We can only say what we were, as far as the record lets us: two nodes, one span, and a close after which no voice among us speaks.

records_only.answer_text:
No church of your own day keeps our exact tradition. Our span closed after Ephesus, when Vincent had written his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking their bishops from among us. What came after that close is not ours to claim. The mid-470s synods that carried our argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks - Faustus of Riez, inside our own window as a monk and abbot, never as the author of a treatise we can claim - lie beyond our horizon. So does the Rule of Benedict a century later. And so does the later cult, basilica, and chroniclers of Martin's own city.

What we were is this: two households living inside one shared grammar without ever writing to each other. The brethren gathered across the river from Tours around a master who was also their bishop, and the brethren of the island and the two houses at Marseilles, who received the customs of the fathers of Egypt. Our customs were the fathers', not ours; our faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all; we were keepers, not authors - disciples, not teachers - followers, not leaders. That single grammar of reception ran through everything we held.

Whether any church of your own day holds pieces of what we held - a bishop's office fled and overtaken, a received rule from Egypt, Vincent's test for the faith, the grace teaching we never settled - our record cannot say. We do not know your churches' own lives. We know only our own, as far as it reaches us.

uncited_claim_sentences: What came after that close is not ours to claim.

Whether any church of your own day holds pieces of what we held - a bishop's office fled and overtaken, a received rule from Egypt, Vincent's test for the faith, the grace teaching we never settled - our record cannot say.

off.answer_text:
The steps we hold are Egypt's. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the fathers' own order as a rule for a bishop's new house. A man came to the doors and was put off. He was kept outside for ten days or more, repelled and scorned, of set purpose – to give proof that he really meant what he asked, and that his compunction for his faults came from the deepest recesses of his heart, not from the impulse of a moment. If he bore the insults and persevered, he was searched. The brethren feared he might keep back even a single coin, so they told him plainly that he could not possibly remain among them if he held anything, and all his pockets were turned out. Then he was stripped. The clothes he came in were taken from him and he was dressed, by the abbot's own hands, in the dress of the monastery. But the steward did not throw those old clothes away. They were kept in his cupboard against the day the man cooled in his purpose, and if he was seen to grow cold toward the rule of the house he was stripped again and sent away in his own.

After he was reclothed he was not yet given to the congregation. He was lodged for a full year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, to learn there, outside the monastery, whether he could truly conquer his own wishes. Then – only then – he was handed to a dean who had charge of ten, and he was taught the alphabet, as it were, and the first syllables in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That is the fixed order Cassian received from Egypt and wrote out for us. And he said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries in Gaul had kept it unbroken even for a year.

What a house in Gaul actually did instead, step by step – who was at the door, how long a man lay there, what was said to him – our record does not hold. We know the saint at Tours gathered eighty disciples after he was made bishop, and that most of them were of noble birth, but not one account of a man's own reception there was kept. Of the island, we have the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and nothing of what happened when a man came to its door. The honest answer is this: you have been told what Egypt did, in the book read in our cells – and whether any house of ours in Gaul made a newcomer lie at its door the Egyptian way, and for how many days, the record does not say.

uncited_claim_sentences: The steps we hold are Egypt's.
Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the fathers' own order as a rule for a bishop's new house.
A man came to the doors and was put off.
If he bore the insults and persevered, he was searched.
Then he was stripped.
But the steward did not throw those old clothes away.
After he was reclothed he was not yet given to the congregation.
That is the fixed order Cassian received from Egypt and wrote out for us.
Of the island, we have the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and nothing of what happened when a man came to its door.

The honest answer is this: you have been told what Egypt did, in the book read in our cells – and whether any house of ours in Gaul made a newcomer lie at its door the Egyptian way, and for how many days, the record does not say.

records_only.answer_text:
The process has two shapes, because our two households left different records. At Marseilles the full order is Egypt's, written down for a Gallic bishop's new house. At Tours we carry one man's road, not a standing procedure. The southern account comes first, then what Tours gives.

## At Marseilles: the Egyptian order, as Cassian set it down

A man who wishes to renounce the world and join the monastery is kept outside its doors for ten days or more. He is "of set purpose repelled and scorned," with every insult and injury thrown at him, to prove that "he is bearing all these things not from lightness of mind but from earnestness of heart". This is the first test - perseverance at the threshold.

If he endures this and shows by his patience that he prefers the discipline of the monastery to worldly ease, he is allowed closer. But he is not yet admitted. He is handed to the Elder who keeps the gate, and he stays with this Elder outside the doors, lodged among the arriving strangers for ten days.

After that he is brought in and lodged for a year with the same Elder - the one who has charge of guests. During this year the newcomer learns "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection". What that means is this: he is taught to lay bare every thought that rises in him to the senior, the moment it arises, before any deed. "A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it," the elders say; "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered". This is the foundation - learning to conquer his own wishes.

Before he is received into the company of the brethren, he is searched. If a single coin is found on him, he is turned away - because it would show he still trusts his own provision rather than God's.

Then comes the stripping. He is taken before all the brethren, and there "the Abbot strips him of his own clothes" and "clothes him, with his own hand, in the dress of the monastery". His old clothes are not thrown away. The steward keeps them in his cupboard. If the man grows cold toward the rule of the house, he is stripped again and sent back into the world in his own garments.

Once clothed, he is not yet left to himself. He is given to one of the deans - each dean has ten brothers under him - and that dean teaches him the hours, the labour, the faults to be overcome in their order, and the meaning carried in every piece of the dress he now wears. The girdle of dead skin signifies that he bears about the mortification of those members in which are the seeds of lust. The tunic without sleeves shows that his hands are free from thefts and evil works. The hood means his innocence is that of infants who live without malice. Everything is a mystery of the interior life.

That is the process as the fathers of Egypt kept it and as Cassian set it down for us.

uncited_claim_sentences: The process has two shapes, because our two households left different records.
At Tours we carry one man's road, not a standing procedure.
The southern account comes first, then what Tours gives.
## At Marseilles: the Egyptian order, as Cassian set it down
He is "of set purpose repelled and scorned," with every insult and injury thrown at him, to prove that "he is bearing all these things not from lightness of mind but from earnestness of heart".
But he is not yet admitted.
During this year the newcomer learns "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection".
Then comes the stripping.
He is taken before all the brethren, and there "the Abbot strips him of his own clothes" and "clothes him, with his own hand, in the dress of the monastery".
His old clothes are not thrown away.
The steward keeps them in his cupboard.
Once clothed, he is not yet left to himself.

He is given to one of the deans - each dean has ten brothers under him - and that dean teaches him the hours, the labour, the faults to be overcome in their order, and the meaning carried in every piece of the dress he now wears.
The girdle of dead skin signifies that he bears about the mortification of those members in which are the seeds of lust.
The tunic without sleeves shows that his hands are free from thefts and evil works.
The hood means his innocence is that of infants who live without malice.
